title: Tactical calculations should not overlook dangers of terror: EAM
where: Politics, page 7 (Shubhajit Roy); The World page for the G20 photo row and the Canada–EU summit
syllabus: GS2 › Important international institutions, agencies and fora (G20); Bilateral, regional and global groupings · GS3 › Terrorism; Security of sea lanes
summary: At the G20 foreign ministers' meeting in Atlanta, Jaishankar warned against tolerating terrorism for tactical gain and spoke for seafarers, freedom of navigation and fair access to markets.
ideas: Terror is not a tool: Jaishankar said tactical calculations should not hide the dangers of terrorism, which has hurt even its practitioners; a veiled reference to US engagement with Pakistan.
GS2 · India's foreign policy / GS3 · Terrorism
India argues that tolerating terrorism for short-term strategic gain backfires on those who use it.
Diplomacy over force: on the wars in Ukraine and West Asia, he said military solutions will not work and diplomacy must be given a chance.
GS2 · International institutions (G20)
India positions itself as a voice for dialogue and diplomacy in today's conflicts.

The Global South pays for shipping attacks: attacks on civilian shipping and seafarers raise the cost of fuel, food and fertiliser; at least 22 Indians, including 14 seafarers, have died in West Asia since February.
GS2 · Global South / GS3 · Maritime security
Attacks on sea lanes hit the Global South hardest through fuel, food and fertiliser prices.
Law of the sea: India called for freedom of navigation and an end to attacks under international law, especially UNCLOS, and has launched a joint initiative with Liberia to protect seafarers.
GS2 · International institutions / Law of the sea
India backs a rules-based maritime order under UNCLOS and acts on seafarer safety with Liberia.
Weaponised trade: he said the right to industrialise is being denied by flooding markets, weaponising supply chains and restricting market access, and urged resilient, alternative connectivity.
GS2 · Groupings / GS3 · Supply chains
India links economic security to de-risking supply chains and building alternative connectivity.
keywords: Using trade, supply chains or market access as coercion
The weaponisation of interdependence makes supply-chain diversification a security need.
Developing countries' claim to build manufacturing without coercion
India frames fair market access as the Global South's right to industrialise.
Right of ships to sail international waters without interference
Freedom of navigation under UNCLOS is central to India's maritime and trade interests.
Reducing over-dependence on single suppliers or partners
As the world de-risks, India pitches itself as a resilient alternative supply base.
Keeping multiple partners to reduce dependence on any one
Canada and the EU seeking closer ties beyond the US reflects strategic hedging.
data: Killed in West Asia since the war began in February
At least 22 Indians, including 14 seafarers, have died in West Asia since February.
examples: India–Liberia seafarer initiative
A joint initiative to safeguard seafarers
GS4
GS2 · Maritime diplomacy / GS4 · Care for workers
India and Liberia's seafarer initiative shows diplomacy protecting ordinary workers at sea.
G20 'family photo' cancelled
The US scrapped the ministers' photo after Europeans objected to being pictured with Russia's Lavrov
GS2 · International institutions (G20)
The scrapped G20 photo shows how the Ukraine war divides the grouping.
Canada–EU 'Alliance for the Future'
Canada and the EU discuss associate membership to cut dependence on the US
GS2 · Groupings / Effect of other countries' policies
Canada's move towards EU associate membership shows middle powers hedging against US unpredictability.
pyqs: Global institutions against terrorism: the UNSC's counter-terror bodies; the G20 is another forum India uses.
The West fostering India as an alternative to China's supply chains.
Challenges as the world moves from multilateralism to protectionism.
Maritime security and freedom of navigation.
BRICS and the voice of the Global South.

trend.t: Groupings questions moved from SAARC and SCO (2016, 2021, 2023) to the Global South and BRICS as a counterweight (2026). Economic security entered through supply chains (2024) and protectionism (2025), while terrorism moved to a global, UN-level frame (2024).
trend.watch: The Global South and supply-chain security have come in each of the last three years. Prepare India's voice in groupings with concrete examples: G20, BRICS, seafarers, de-risking.
focus: India as voice of the Global South
Maritime security, UNCLOS and sea lanes

potential: "Economic security has become inseparable from national security." Discuss with reference to supply chains and sea lanes. (15 marks)
How has India used the G20 to raise the concerns of the Global South? Illustrate with recent examples. (10 marks)
Assess the effectiveness of the G20 as a forum for global governance amid great-power rivalry. (10 marks)

practice.q: How has India used the G20 to raise the concerns of the Global South? Illustrate with recent examples.

answer.t: At the G20 foreign ministers' meeting in Atlanta, India said the Global South is disproportionately bearing the cost of attacks on shipping and seafarers.

pts.t: Disrupted sea lanes raise costs for developing economies.
At least 22 Indians, including 14 seafarers, have died in West Asia.
Freedom of navigation under UNCLOS.
Against market flooding and weaponised supply chains.
No tactical tolerance for terror.
Military solutions will not work; diplomacy must get a chance.
Work with BRICS, the African Union and like-minded states.
Alternative corridors and diversified supply chains.
Naval and coast-guard cooperation for sea lanes.

answer.t: India's G20 voice turns the Global South's everyday costs into an agenda for rules, routes and fair trade.

title: Ready to share 'battle-tested' anti-terror expertise: Rajnath
syllabus: GS2 › Important international institutions, agencies and fora; India and its neighbourhood (extended neighbourhood); Bilateral, regional and global groupings · GS3 › Terrorism; Security challenges: maritime security · GS4 › Ethics in international relations
summary: At the ASEAN Defence Ministers' Meeting-Plus in Cebu, Rajnath Singh offered India's counter-terror experience to ASEAN and its partners and called India a trusted net security provider in the Indo-Pacific.
ideas: Counter-terrorism as defence diplomacy: India offers practical counter-terror expertise to ADMM-Plus partners through joint exercises, capacity building and intelligence sharing, drawn from decades of facing cross-border terror.
GS2 groupings / extended neighbourhood · GS3 terrorism
India's offer of counter-terror cooperation to ADMM-Plus partners adds a security pillar to its engagement with the extended neighbourhood.

A clear stand against state-sponsored terror: Operation Sindoor was presented as a declaration of India's approach to state-sponsored terrorism, taking India's position on Pakistan-backed terror to a multilateral forum.
GS3 terrorism · GS2 India–Pakistan
By projecting Operation Sindoor at ADMM-Plus, India seeks global consensus against state sponsors of terrorism.
Statements are not enough: with some maritime trade routes facing new threats, Rajnath said statements on maritime security are insufficient and called for practical collective action.
GS3 · Maritime security
Protecting sea lanes needs collective capability, not just declarations on freedom of navigation.
Net security provider: India will continue as a trusted net security provider in the Indian Ocean region and the wider Indo-Pacific.
GS2 · Indian Ocean / Indo-Pacific
As a net security provider, India seeks to shape, not just benefit from, security in the Indian Ocean.
Peace as collective work: India backs a secure, resilient Indo-Pacific where peace and stability come from collective effort, not mere aspiration.
GS2 · Indo-Pacific vision
India's Indo-Pacific vision rests on collective effort through ASEAN-led and partner platforms.
keywords: A country that provides security for its region, not just itself
India positions itself as the Indian Ocean's net security provider.
Using defence cooperation as a tool of foreign policy
Defence diplomacy has given Act East a security dimension.
Terror backed by a state as a tool of policy
India is building global consensus against state-sponsored terrorism.
ASEAN-led forums at the core of Indo-Pacific architecture
India's support for ASEAN centrality anchors its Indo-Pacific policy.
Disruptions to SLOCs make maritime security a shared regional concern.
Small groups of like-minded countries cooperating
Sideline talks with Japan and Australia reflect India's minilateral approach.
examples: ADMM-Plus
ASEAN-led forum of ASEAN defence ministers and dialogue partners, including India
GS2 · International institutions and fora
ADMM-Plus is a key ASEAN-led platform for India's security engagement with its extended neighbourhood.
Operation Sindoor at a multilateral forum
Presented as India's declaration against state-sponsored terror
GS3 · Terrorism / GS2 India–Pakistan
India projected Operation Sindoor at ADMM-Plus to build consensus against state-sponsored terror.
Talks with Japan and Australia
Rajnath met his Japanese and Australian counterparts on the sidelines
GS2 · Quad partners / minilateralism
Sideline talks with Japan and Australia show minilateral coordination among Indo-Pacific partners.
Offer to share counter-terror experience
India offers exercises, training and intelligence sharing to partners facing terror
GS4
GS4 · Leadership and empathy in international relations
Sharing hard-won counter-terror experience reflects responsible leadership and solidarity with nations facing terror.
pyqs: Strategic dimensions of Look East: defence diplomacy at ADMM-Plus is its security side today.
Maritime security for sea trade: disruptions to trade routes and collective action.
SAGAR and Quad's Indo-Pacific strategy: India as net security provider.
Cross-border terrorism and regional forums: India now takes this concern to ASEAN-led platforms.

trend.t: Questions moved from South China Sea disputes (2014) and Look East (2016) to Indo-Pacific security architecture: defence deals and stability (2020), AUKUS (2021), Maldives and maritime security (2024–25) and IPMDA linking SAGAR with the Quad (2026). The shift of trade to the Indo-Pacific came in GS1 in 2026.
trend.watch: The Indo-Pacific and maritime security have come in 2020, 2021, 2024, 2025 and 2026. It is a must-study area across GS1, GS2 and GS3.
focus: Act East and ASEAN-led security forums
India as net security provider; SAGAR and IPMDA

potential: "India's Act East Policy has steadily acquired a security dimension." Discuss in the context of India's engagement with ASEAN-led forums. (15 marks)
What does India's role as a 'net security provider' in the Indian Ocean region entail? Examine its opportunities and challenges. (10 marks)
How can regional forums strengthen global cooperation against state-sponsored terrorism? Discuss with reference to India. (10 marks)

practice.q: What does India's role as a 'net security provider' in the Indian Ocean region entail? Examine its opportunities and challenges.
parts: Introduction: the ADMM-Plus statement in one line

answer.t: At ADMM-Plus in Cebu (October 2026), India reaffirmed its role as a trusted net security provider in the Indian Ocean and wider Indo-Pacific.

pts.t: Protecting trade routes against piracy, terror and disruption.
Training, joint exercises and equipment for smaller littoral states.
pts.ex: Offer of counter-terror expertise to ADMM-Plus partners.

pts.t: Humanitarian assistance and disaster relief across the region.
Coordination with ASEAN, Japan, Australia and other partners.
pts.ex: Sideline talks with Japan and Australia.

pts.t: Expanding Chinese footprint and dual-use ports in the region.
Limited naval assets for a vast ocean space.
Small states wary of dependence on any one power.
Terrorism, trafficking and climate disasters stretch resources.
Expand naval and maritime domain awareness capacity.
Work through ASEAN-led and partner frameworks, respecting ASEAN centrality.
Combine security with SAGAR's growth agenda.

answer.t: India's credibility as a net security provider will rest on capability backed by trust in its partners.
